Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We present the first X-ray detection of the very young pulsar PSR J1357-6429 (characteristic age of 7.3 kyr) using data from the XMM-Newton and Chandra satellites. We find that the spectrum is well described by a power-law plus blackbody model, with photon index Gamma=1.4 and blackbody temperature kT=160 eV. For the estimated distance of 2.5 kpc, this corresponds to a 2-10 keV luminosity of about 1.2E+32 erg/s, thus the fraction of the spin-down energy channeled by PSR J1357-6429 into X-ray emission is one of the lowest observed. The Chandra data confirm the positional coincidence with the radio pulsar and allow to set an upper limit of 3E+31 erg/s on the 2-10 keV luminosity of a compact pulsar wind nebula. We do not detect any pulsed emission from the source and determine an upper limit of 30% for the modulation amplitude of the X-ray emission at the radio frequency of the pulsar.

outputs.L1: We report the first X-ray detection of the very young pulsar PSR J1357−6429, which has a characteristic age of 7.3 kyr, using observations from the XMM-Newton and Chandra satellites. We find that its spectrum is well described by a power-law plus blackbody model, with a photon index of Γ = 1.4 and a blackbody temperature of kT = 160 eV. Assuming an estimated distance of 2.5 kpc, this corresponds to a 2–10 keV luminosity of approximately 1.2 × 10^32 erg s^−1, indicating that the fraction of spin-down energy channeled by PSR J1357−6429 into X-ray emission is among the lowest observed. The Chandra data confirm the positional coincidence with the radio pulsar and allow us to place an upper limit of 3 × 10^31 erg s^−1 on the 2–10 keV luminosity of a compact pulsar wind nebula. We detect no pulsed emission from the source and derive an upper limit of 30% for the modulation amplitude of the X-ray emission at the pulsar’s radio frequency.
outputs.L2: Using observations from the XMM-Newton and Chandra space telescopes, we report the first detection in X-rays of the extremely young pulsar PSR J1357-6429, which has a characteristic age of 7.3 kyr. Its spectrum is fitted well by a model combining a power-law component and a blackbody component, with a photon index of Gamma = 1.4 and a blackbody temperature of kT = 160 eV. Assuming the pulsar lies at the estimated distance of 2.5 kpc, its luminosity in the 2–10 keV band is approximately 1.2E+32 erg/s. This indicates that PSR J1357-6429 converts an exceptionally small fraction of its spin-down power into X-ray radiation compared with most observed pulsars. The Chandra observations verify that the X-ray position matches that of the radio pulsar and make it possible to place an upper bound of 3E+31 erg/s on the 2–10 keV luminosity of any compact pulsar wind nebula. No pulsed X-ray signal is detected from the source; at the pulsar’s radio frequency, the modulation amplitude of the X-ray emission is constrained to be below 30%.
outputs.L3:
The study presents the first X-ray detection of the very young pulsar PSR J1357-6429, based on observations obtained with the XMM-Newton and Chandra X-ray observatories. These data provide the first opportunity to characterize the high-energy emission from this pulsar and to compare its X-ray properties with those of other young rotation-powered neutron stars.

The observed X-ray spectrum of PSR J1357-6429 is well described by a model consisting of a non-thermal power-law component plus a thermal blackbody component. The power-law component has a photon index of approximately 1.4, indicating relatively hard X-ray emission, while the blackbody component has a temperature of about 160 eV. This combination suggests that the pulsar’s X-ray emission likely includes both magnetospheric radiation and thermal emission from the neutron star surface or heated polar regions.

Assuming an estimated distance of 2.5 kpc, the pulsar’s luminosity in the 2–10 keV energy band is approximately \(1.2 \times 10^{32}\) erg s\(^{-1}\). Compared with its rotational energy loss rate, this implies a very low X-ray conversion efficiency. In fact, PSR J1357-6429 appears to be among the least efficient young pulsars known in terms of converting spin-down power into X-ray emission.

The Chandra observations provide improved spatial resolution and confirm that the detected X-ray source is positionally coincident with the known radio pulsar. These data also allow constraints to be placed on any compact pulsar wind nebula surrounding the neutron star. No clear compact nebular emission is detected, and the luminosity of any such pulsar wind nebula is limited to less than about \(3 \times 10^{31}\) erg s\(^{-1}\).

Finally, the study searches for X-ray pulsations at the known radio frequency of PSR J1357-6429. No pulsed X-ray emission is detected. The observations place an upper limit of approximately 30% on the modulation amplitude, meaning that any X-ray pulsations present at the radio period must be weaker than this level.
outputs.L4:
The study presents the first detection of X-ray emission from the very young and energetic pulsar PSR J1357-6429. Observations obtained with the XMM-Newton and Chandra X-ray observatories reveal a faint X-ray source coincident with the radio position of the pulsar. The data are analyzed spectrally, and the emission is found to be best described by a combination of a non-thermal power-law component and a thermal blackbody component. This suggests that the observed X-rays may include both magnetospheric emission from the pulsar and thermal radiation from a hot region on the neutron-star surface.

Despite the pulsar’s large spin-down power, its measured X-ray output is relatively weak. In the 2–10 keV energy band, the luminosity is estimated to be approximately \(1.2 \times 10^{32}\) erg s\(^{-1}\). This corresponds to a very low efficiency for converting rotational spin-down energy into X-ray radiation, making PSR J1357-6429 unusually underluminous in X-rays compared with many other young, energetic pulsars.

The timing analysis does not reveal significant X-ray pulsations from the source. As a result, the study reports no detected pulsed emission and can only place limits on the pulsed fraction. In addition, the high-resolution Chandra data show no clear evidence for a compact pulsar wind nebula surrounding the pulsar. The absence of such extended emission allows the authors to place a stringent upper limit on the luminosity of any compact nebula that might be present. Overall, the observations show that PSR J1357-6429 is an X-ray-faint young pulsar, with weak or undetected pulsed emission and little evidence for a bright surrounding pulsar wind nebula.
outputs.L5:
PSR sources, short for pulsars, are highly magnetized rotating neutron stars that emit beams of electromagnetic radiation. As they spin, these beams can sweep across Earth, producing regular pulses that are detected at radio, optical, X-ray, or gamma-ray wavelengths. Because of their extreme density, strong magnetic fields, and precise rotation periods, pulsars are important objects for studying fundamental physics, stellar evolution, and the behavior of matter under extreme conditions.

XMM-Newton is a major space observatory operated by the European Space Agency. Launched in 1999, it is designed to observe the universe in X-rays with high sensitivity. Its powerful instruments allow astronomers to study energetic cosmic objects such as black holes, galaxy clusters, supernova remnants, and neutron stars, including PSR systems.

When XMM-Newton observes a PSR, it can measure the X-ray emission coming from the pulsar itself, from hot regions on its surface, or from surrounding structures such as pulsar wind nebulae. These observations help scientists understand how pulsars lose energy, how particles are accelerated in their magnetic fields, and how neutron stars cool over time. In some cases, XMM-Newton data can also reveal variations in brightness that match the pulsar’s rotation period.

Together, PSR studies and XMM-Newton observations provide valuable insight into some of the most extreme environments in the universe. By combining X-ray data from XMM-Newton with observations from radio and gamma-ray telescopes, astronomers can build a more complete picture of pulsars and their role in the cosmos.

The source is detected as a point-like counterpart at the radio position, with no significant extended emission. Its spectrum is well described by an absorbed power-law model, with photon index Γ ≈ 1.5 and hydrogen column density NH ≈ few × 10²¹ cm⁻²; a thermal component is not required by the data. The unabsorbed 0.5–10 keV luminosity is LX ≈ 10³² d²₂.₅ erg s⁻¹, corresponding to an X-ray efficiency of order 10⁻⁵–10⁻⁴ relative to the spin-down power. Chandra imaging places a stringent upper limit on any compact pulsar wind nebula, LPWN ≲ few × 10³¹ d²₂.₅ erg s⁻¹. A search for X-ray pulsations at the radio period yields no significant detection, with an upper limit on the pulsed fraction of roughly 30–40%, depending on energy band and pulse shape. These observations establish PSR J1357−6429 as a faint but typical young rotation-powered X-ray pulsar.

The high angular resolution Chandra data resolve compact X-ray emission associated with the pulsar from surrounding diffuse emission, while the XMM-Newton data provide improved spectral constraints. The pulsar spectrum is well described by a combination of non-thermal magnetospheric emission and a soft thermal component, with a photon index \(\Gamma = 1.4\) and blackbody temperature \(kT = 160\) eV. counterfactuals.output: **Abstract** — We report the first detection of X-ray emission from the young, energetic radio pulsar PSR J1357−6429. The source is detected at the radio timing position as a hard, absorbed X-ray point source, consistent with non-thermal magnetospheric emission from a rotation-powered pulsar. Spectral fits are adequately described by an absorbed power law, with parameters typical of young pulsars, and imply an X-ray luminosity that is a small fraction of the pulsar spin-down power, confirming PSR J1357−6429 as an inefficient but otherwise ordinary X-ray emitter among high-\(\dot{E}\) neutron stars. No statistically significant X-ray pulsations are detected at the radio period; the data constrain the pulsed fraction to be below the level of roughly a few tens of per cent, depending on the assumed pulse profile and background treatment. The available angular resolution also limits any unresolved or compact pulsar-wind nebula contribution: extended emission on scales comparable to the instrumental point-spread function cannot dominate the measured flux, and any compact PWN must contribute no more than a modest fraction of the total X-ray emission. These results establish PSR J1357−6429 as an X-ray pulsar candidate and provide initial constraints on its magnetospheric emission, compact nebular environment, and high-energy beaming geometry, motivating deeper, high-time-resolution observations with sub-arcsecond imaging to separate the pulsar and nebular components and to search more sensitively for X-ray pulsations.

**Abstract**

We report the first detection of X-ray emission from the young radio pulsar PSR J1357−6429 using *XMM-Newton* and *Chandra* observations. PSR J1357−6429 is a 7.3 kyr-old neutron star, making it a promising target for studies of early pulsar evolution and high-energy emission. The X-ray spectrum is well described by a composite power-law plus blackbody model, with a photon index of \(\Gamma \simeq 1.4\) and a thermal component characterized by \(kT \simeq 160\) eV. Assuming a distance of 2.5 kpc, the inferred X-ray luminosity is \(L_X \simeq 1.2 \times 10^{32}\) erg s\(^{-1}\). No significant extended emission attributable to a pulsar wind nebula is detected; we place an upper limit of \(L_X \lesssim 3 \times 10^{31}\) erg s\(^{-1}\) on any associated nebular emission. Timing analysis yields no significant X-ray pulsations, with an upper limit on the pulsed fraction of approximately 30%. These results establish PSR J1357−6429 as a faint but detectable X-ray pulsar and provide constraints on its surface thermal emission, magnetospheric activity, and possible pulsar wind nebula.
